clinicalPearls: A drug-induced eruption that clinically and histologically mimics idiopathic lichen planus, with violaceous flat-topped papules and plaques
Compared with classic lichen planus it tends to be more widespread and symmetrical, may favour sun-exposed sites, and Wickham striae and mucosal involvement are often less prominent
There is characteristically a latent period of weeks to months between starting the drug and the onset of the eruption, which can hamper recognition
Frequently implicated drugs include certain antihypertensives, antimalarials, diuretics, gold, and increasingly immune checkpoint inhibitors and other biologic agents
Healing often leaves marked post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, particularly in more pigmented skin
Histology resembles lichen planus but may show more eosinophils, parakeratosis and a deeper, more perivascular infiltrate as clues to a drug cause
The eruption typically improves after the culprit drug is withdrawn, though resolution can be slow over weeks to months
Management is identification and withdrawal of the responsible drug together with topical or, if extensive, systemic corticosteroids and symptomatic measures
reference.pathophysiology: Lichenoid drug eruption is a T-cell-mediated interface reaction in which a drug or its metabolite triggers a cytotoxic lymphocytic attack on basal keratinocytes. The resulting band-like (lichenoid) infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction, with basal cell degeneration and apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies), reproduces the histological pattern of lichen planus. The drug is thought to act as a hapten or to alter self-antigens so that basal keratinocytes are recognised as foreign, and the relatively long latent period reflects the time required for sensitisation. Damage to basal cells releases melanin that is taken up by dermal macrophages, accounting for the prominent residual pigmentation.
additionalDifferentials: Lichenoid keratosis and hypertrophic lichenoid dermatoses
Pityriasis rosea and other papulosquamous eruptions
Photodistributed drug eruption when photoexposed sites are involved
additionalInvestigations: Detailed drug history noting agents started weeks to months before onset
Skin biopsy demonstrating a lichenoid interface dermatitis, with features suggesting a drug cause
Review of temporal relationship between drug introduction, withdrawal and improvement
Autoimmune serology to help exclude lupus in photodistributed cases
Assessment of mucosae and nails to compare with idiopathic lichen planus
Patch testing in selected cases to support identification of the culprit
redFlags: Extensive or erythrodermic involvement requiring urgent assessment
Painful or erosive mucosal disease impairing function
Eruption associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy needing oncology liaison
Failure to improve after drug withdrawal, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The eruption usually resolves after the responsible drug is stopped, although clearance may take several weeks to months and often leaves lasting hyperpigmentation; recurrence follows re-exposure to the culprit drug.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the long latent period and therefore not linking the eruption to a drug
Mistaking it for idiopathic lichen planus and missing the treatable drug cause
Expecting rapid clearance and stopping investigation prematurely
Overlooking newer agents such as checkpoint inhibitors as triggers
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on cutaneous drug reactions
management: Identify and withdraw the culprit drug (antihypertensives, antimalarials, diuretics, gold, immune checkpoint inhibitors or other biologics) as the definitive step
Prescribe potent topical corticosteroids for localised disease, with a short course of systemic corticosteroids for widespread eruption
Consider phototherapy in selected persistent cases
Advise photoprotection and reassurance for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, which fades slowly
Document the culprit agent to avoid re-exposure, which provokes recurrence, and liaise with the prescriber to find an alternative for the original indication
